are set in, and — this pack alone under the heading — whether they

_comment_title: Where this show parts company with the four packs cut to the same
design. Hall of Femme sets its captions in Telegraf — a 200-weight
hairline for the block, the 800 for a picked word — on a hot pink
card. Fitness Story uses HK Grotesk on an electric blue one,
Determined uses Open Sans on acid yellow, Fight Source uses Open Sans
on black or white. This one is set in Arial Bold, with the bold
italic for a picked word, on a card that is black, white or a single
muted red — and it is the only pack under this heading that does not
uppercase what the user typed.
Arial is the decision the rest of the pack follows from, and it is a
deliberately unglamorous one. The four siblings each reach for a
typeface with a voice — a hairline, a humanist sans, a geometric —
because their captions are the only graphic in the frame. A show
about food is looking at the food: the caption's job is to name what
is on screen and then get out of the way, and Arial Bold at 40px is
about the most legible way to put a short sentence over a picture
that anybody has shipped. It is also on every machine that will ever
open this app, which is what makes the next paragraph possible.
It is declared inline and with no file, because it is not a font
this app ships. `file` is null and `css` false to say so outright —
nothing is registered for it (see channels.registerFace, which skips
a face with no file) and it is reached by name. fontguard still
verifies that something real answers to that name before a single
line is measured, so a machine that somehow lacks Arial says so
instead of quietly laying the block out against a fallback.

_comment_face: Arial at bold, which is a WEIGHT of the family rather than a
family of its own — the opposite of the case a face like Arial
Black presents, which has to be asked for by NAME because it is
its own family and asking Arial for 900 would only invite a
browser to synthesise one. Here the cut genuinely
exists: every machine that has Arial has Arial Bold, and `bold`
is how you reach it.
The stack falls back through Helvetica before the generic, which
is the one fallback in this codebase that is not merely damage
limitation. Helvetica is metrically compatible with Arial — the
same advance widths, glyph for glyph — so a machine that somehow
had one and not the other would lay this block out to the same
numbers rather than to Impact's. It is still a fallback and
fontguard still refuses to draw against one; it is just the only
one here that would not be a lie.
_comment_uppercase: Off, and this pack is the only one under the Snapchat heading
where it is. What the user types is what the canvas sets, capital
for capital.
The argument every sibling makes for capitals is a real one, and
it is an argument about their faces rather than about captions in
general. Hall of Femme is set in a 200-weight hairline, and a
hairline lower-case at caption size is the one setting where it
genuinely disappears — capitals give it stems the eye can find.
Arial Bold has no such problem: it is a 700-weight grotesque
whose lower-case is as solid as its capitals, so uppercasing it
would buy nothing and cost the two things below.
The first is that a food show's captions are full of names that
carry their own casing — a dish, a restaurant, a chef, a place —
and a name flattened into capitals is a name the reader has to
reconstruct. Those names arrive from the rewrite rather than from
somebody typing them (see backend/narrator.py), so the casing in
the text box is information that was produced on purpose, and
throwing it away at the draw would be throwing away the more
considered of the two.
The second is reading speed, which is the whole job here. A line
of capitals is a rectangle; a line of mixed case has ascenders
and descenders sticking out of it, and word shape is most of how
a sentence is read at a glance on a phone. Twenty characters is a
glance either way, and mixed case is the faster glance.
It is applied at the draw and not to what is stored, so turning
it off changes only what the canvas does: the text box held the
user's own casing all along, and the highlight buttons already
offered the words as the canvas would set them (see the `cased`
note in js/text.js and editor.renderWordButtons). Which is why
nothing downstream of this key needed to know it had changed.
_comment_color: The channel's own answer, and therefore what every frame is set
in until somebody presses a swatch: a frame stores no colour of
its own until it is given one, and this is what it falls back to
(see state.textColorFor). It is one of the three in `colors`
below, so the white swatch is the one that shows as chosen on an
untouched frame — the swatch is found by matching this value
rather than by being listed first.
White letters on the black card is what this show opens on. Black
is the bigger surface — a fifth of the frame, read before
anything set on it — and against food, which is what every still
on this channel is going to be warm and bright with, a black card
is the one ground that neither competes with the plate nor gets
lost in it. White is what is unambiguously legible on it at every
size. The red, and the same card the other way round, are a
_comment_colors: The three colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and
for the slab behind them — three buttons each in the title panel
(see editor.renderColorButtons). Nothing counts the lists, so a
row of three is a row of three; see `colors` in
content/README.md.
The same three in both lists, in one order, which is what every
pack under this heading does and for their reason: the point is
the PAIRING, and two rows written the same way read as one palette
offered twice rather than as two unrelated sets.
Two of the three are the ends of the range and the third is the
brand. Fight Source's note explains why the black and the white
are absolute rather than a #111 and a #FAFAFA, and every word of
it applies here: a near-black that reads as black on a monitor
becomes a grey slab beside a genuinely black picture on a phone,
and an off-white card that is a card on a monitor is a dirty one
against a blown highlight. The card is a flat shape, not a
photograph seen through it, so there is nothing for either extreme
to be too harsh against.
The red is what makes this a show rather than a default. It is a
muted one and not a signal red — nearer a brick than a warning —
which is the only kind that can be BOTH ink and card, and being
both is the whole of what this palette asks of a colour. At Fight
Source's contrast a hot red as type on white would vibrate and the
same red as a card would fight the food; at this one it is dark
enough to carry white letters and light enough to be read as
letters on the white. It is also, on a channel whose frames are
cut from cooking footage, the one hue that belongs to what is on
screen rather than being laid over it.
Six of the nine combinations are worth having and three of them
are a rectangle — black on black, white on white, red on red.
Nothing stops the user choosing one, and that is not an oversight:
the two lists are independent because the pairing is the feature,
and a rule barring the three matching combinations would cost the
panel more explaining than an invisible caption costs the user,
who can see it is invisible and presses another swatch.
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block — see the note
on `colors` in js/channels.js. This channel's highlight is a
different CUT of the face and not a different colour, so what
colour the type is has one answer and not two.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in Arial Bold Italic, in the same colour as
the rest of the block. The colour it names is the block's, so the
recolour draws exactly what its neighbours are drawn in and the
face is the whole of the difference. Stated all the same, for the
fallback reason `color` above is stated — and moved to white with
it, since a highlight that changed colour as well as slant would
be two highlights.
The slant rather than a heavier cut, as on Fitness Story and
Fight Source, and here there is no second option to weigh: the
block is already bold, and this family's next step up is Arial
Black, which is a different family with different proportions
rather than a heavier weight of this one. Leaning the word is the
change this face can make cleanly, and at 40px on a flat ground
with nothing else moving it is enough.
It reads harder here than on either sibling, for a reason that is
this pack's alone: with `uppercase` off, an italic lower-case
carries a change of letterform as well as of angle — Arial's
italic a and e are drawn differently, not merely slanted — so a
picked word is doing two things at once where a picked word in
capitals could only ever lean.
Word scope, the same as all six of its neighbours, and for their
reason: a caption's line breaks are wherever the sentence happened
to run out of width, so picking a line out picks out a fragment
rather than a thought. The words are what carry meaning, and the
one worth leaning — a dish, a number, the verb the clip turns on —
sits in the middle of a line as often as it fills one. A row whose
picked words are in another face is built out of runs, each
measured and drawn in its own face at the pen the runs before it
reached (see `runRows` in js/text.js), which is what lets the face
change at a word and costs the kerning across each join.
Mode is colour rather than box because there is nothing to box
against — the words are already on a solid ground of their own —
so the highlight here is the SLANT, on a card that stays one clean
rectangle.

_comment_face: The italic cut of the same family, and the one place in this
pack where the data is doing something that needs explaining
rather than merely stating.
There is no `style` key on a face, and adding one would be a
worse answer than this. Every measurement and every draw in
the renderer builds one CSS font shorthand out of two fields —
`${weight} ${size}px ${stack}` — at the raw canvas (the four
measuring contexts in js/text.js) and through fabric, which
prepends its own `normal` font-style in front of the same
weight. Nothing reads a third field. So a `style` key invented
here would reach the drawn text and not the measurements, or
the reverse, and a block laid out against one cut and painted
in another is precisely the failure fontguard exists to catch
— self-inflicted this time, and invisible until somebody
notices the boxes are the wrong width.
So the slant travels in `weight`, as `italic bold`. That is
not a trick played on the shorthand, it is the shorthand: CSS
lets font-style, font-variant, font-weight and font-stretch
appear in any order in front of the size, and a leading
`normal` from fabric is skipped rather than fighting the
`italic` behind it. Both strings therefore parse to the same
font — and, which is the actual point, they are the SAME
string, so what is measured and what is drawn cannot come
apart.
It is worth the paragraph because it looks like a mistake. A
field called `weight` holding two words is the kind of thing
somebody tidies up on a quiet afternoon. The alternative is a
`style` field, four call sites in text.js and a fabric
property to keep in step with them, for one channel — against
content/README.md's whole claim, which is that a channel is a
folder that gets dropped in.
The family is `Arial` and not `Arial Bold Italic`, unlike rift
or hanken-grotesk-italic, and the difference is that those
ship a FILE holding one cut, which has to be named exactly or
another cut of the family answers to it. Arial arrives with
the machine as a family and its cuts are reached by weight and
style rather than by name, so asking for `Arial Bold Italic`
as a family would find nothing at all.
One consequence, and it is the right one: because both faces
are family `Arial`, text.titleFaces collapses them into a
single face to verify and fontguard caches its answer under
that one family. That dedup was written for a pack that named
the same face twice, and it is correct here for a better
reason — `is Arial on this machine` has one answer, and asking
it twice would not make it two.

_comment_panel: The card the caption is set on, in whichever of the three colours
the frame is wearing. Every number in it is hall-of-femme's, and
the long argument for each is there rather than repeated here:
one box per LINE and `joined`, so the background is a single shape
that steps in and out with the sentence instead of a rectangle the
width of its longest line; 12 of padding, which is a highlighter's
margin and not a card's; no border, because a keyline would make
the slab read as a box drawn over the picture rather than as a
card lying on it; 13 of corner radius, the number every background
under this heading is rounded by; and a soft shadow falling
straight down, which has to survive being thrown by a white slab
onto a white wall — a case this pack can actually produce, since
white is a third of its palette.
One thing the line boxes do that no sibling has had to think about,
because this is the first pack under the heading with descenders
in it. Every box in a block takes ONE shared vertical band, the
union of what every row needs, so the boxes differ in width and in
nothing else — a line ending in a g does not get a taller box than
the line above it (see the band in js/text.js). What the band does
do is grow for the block as a whole, so a caption containing a
descender is carried on a card a few pixels deeper than one that
happens not to. That is the one price mixed case pays and capitals
do not; it is smaller than the shadow under the card, and it buys
the reading speed `uppercase` above is about.
The fill is the one line here that is this show's own, and it is
black. This and `color` above are also the only place the opening
look is stated: the two lists in `colors` are written in one order
so the two rows of buttons read as the same palette twice, which
means neither of them can decide what an untouched frame wears.
